b: Thursday, November 19, 2026 was a day of price tags and fine print. Bending Spoons agreed to buy Mailchimp from Intuit for $3.68bn in cash, about a third of what Intuit paid five years ago. The two largest American retail media businesses after Amazon both reported slower advertising growth: Walmart's global ad sales rose 25%, its weakest pace in two years, and Target's ad revenue grew 23% to $296m. A holiday study found Amazon draws a quarter of retailer searches but appears in only about a tenth of AI shopping answers, and a SparkToro analysis put the share of ChatGPT conversations showing purchase intent at 6.9%. Microsoft said its new Discover feed carries 35% fewer ads per page than MSN, Google kept testing how ads look inside AI Mode, and Nielsen will soon credit a radio listener after a single minute. Apple let apps send the Global Privacy Control signal, Minnesota settled its first privacy case, Spain told companies that marketing chiefs should not be data protection officers, and a Colombian court upheld orders against Google over teenagers' data. Nike explained why it wants creators to build its brand, a Daily Mail sales unit set out to represent its own creators, and Spanish advertisers paused TikTok after reports of abuse material on the platform. The thread running through the day was proof: buyers, regulators and courts asked for evidence where they used to accept assurances.

The Landline newsletter can also be heard. Marketing Is Calling reads each edition aloud every day, on Spotify, Apple Podcasts and YouTube. Marketing Rodeo picks the most controversial advertising story of each day, weekends included, and has some fun with it, on Spotify, Apple Podcasts and YouTube.

Walmart's advertising engine is still growing fast, just less fast than before. PPC Land reported that Walmart's global ad growth dropped to 25% as Flipkart's sale slipped a quarter. In the third quarter of fiscal 2027, the three months to October 31, global advertising grew 25%, down from 38% in the previous quarter. Most of the slowdown came from abroad: international advertising fell 15% because India's Flipkart Big Billion Days sale moved into the fourth quarter. In the United States, advertising grew 37% including VIZIO and Vibe.co, and Walmart Connect on its own rose 36%, down from 43%. Adweek reported that Walmart saw its weakest global ad sales growth in two years, the slowest since the first quarter of 2024 and well below the 53% recorded a year earlier.

The numbers around advertising explain why it matters so much to the company. Total revenue reached $188.8bn, up 5.2%, while net income fell 19.5%, mainly because of an investment loss tied to Symbotic. US ecommerce sales grew 23% and marketplace net sales 49%. John David Rainey, the chief financial officer, said US ecommerce was close to paying for itself without ad income: "we are actually getting to a point where we are pretty close to break-even without advertising, which was pretty remarkable." Seth Dallaire, chief growth officer, pointed to televisions as a new front: "The TVs that are powered by VIZIO OS have been the number one sellers in the U.S." Walmart raised its full-year guidance for the second time and launched a $120 bundle of Walmart+ and Sam's Club Plus on October 20, but it still does not disclose advertising revenue in dollars.

Target, which does disclose a figure, showed a similar shape. PPC Land reported that Target's ad revenue climbed 23% to $296m in the third quarter, up from $241m, for the three months to October 31. Over nine months, advertising revenue reached $821m, up 32.2%, so the third quarter grew more slowly than the first half. Net sales rose 7.1% to $27.1bn and comparable sales rose 5.6%. Diluted earnings of $2.65 a share included $0.50 from $301m in tariff refunds, which flatters the underlying profit picture. Target also books some activity from Roundel, its ad network, as cost reductions rather than revenue, which makes clean comparisons with rivals harder. "Our investments are building on one another," said Michael Fiddelke, the chief executive.

The holiday data suggests the retailers' search dominance does not carry over neatly into AI assistants. PPC Land reported that Amazon draws 24% of retailer searches but 11% of AI shopping answers, in a 30-page US holiday report from Verve, the ad tech company that owns Captify, covering September 1 to November 16. Walmart had 12% of searches and 9% of answers, Target 5% and 8%, and Best Buy and eBay 2% and 3% each. The report did not explain the gap, named no AI platforms and included no sales data, and it cautioned that "a mention is not a recommendation." AI prompts were also far longer than searches: the median AI gift prompt ran 24 words against nine for a gift search, and 7.2% of AI gift prompts stated a budget, against 0.49% of searches, with a median stated budget of $50.

Amazon kept documenting its new buying tools. PPC Land reported that Amazon's DVA+ frequency caps count Netflix and Prime Video as one. A Support Center page updated on November 19 says a single counter tracks each viewer's impressions across every publisher a campaign buys. "Frequency caps apply across multiple publishers and supply sources," the page says. Private auctions and preferred deals are fully enforced, but some programmatic guaranteed deals count towards the cap and keep delivering after it, and Twitch share-of-voice lines and Fire tablet ads sit outside caps altogether. PPC Land found Amazon's worked example off by one and two of its three savings formulas inconsistent with their stated units.

A second page sets the rules for what a campaign is for. PPC Land reported that Amazon's DVA+ primer lists 15 KPIs, with one goal per campaign. Each campaign has one goal, one budget and one KPI inherited by every ad group, so an awareness push and a sales push need separate campaigns. The three goals are awareness, consideration and conversion, and Amazon warns that changing a KPI after launch resets a campaign's performance learnings and may affect optimisation. The page names five display ad types, caps standard display at ten image assets and uses both "DVA+" and "Amazon Ads Agent" for the same product in different places.

Brands get a simpler tool in their own stores. PPC Land reported that Amazon's free Brand Store quiz narrows up to 50 products with four questions. The Product Selector module, listed in 25 marketplaces, asks shoppers up to four questions with up to six answers each and shows only products that match every answer. "Product Selector is free, self-service, and requires no minimum spend," Amazon says. The logic is rule-based, since brands assign products to answers by hand, which is a contrast with Rufus, where Amazon's models choose. Early agency write-ups described a beta capped at 35 products and three questions.

Walmart also published a reminder that its stores double as clinics, and clinics bring shoppers. PPC Land reported that nearly three in four Walmart test-and-treat visits come after 5 p.m. or on weekends. The service, where pharmacists can test for flu, strep throat and COVID-19, prescribe and fill in one visit, runs at more than 1,500 of roughly 4,600 Walmart pharmacies in 24 states. "Our pharmacists are often one of the most accessible healthcare professionals in the communities we serve," said Kevin Host, senior vice president of pharmacy for Walmart US. PPC Land noted that pharmacy visits are also store visits that feed Walmart Connect, while health records remain subject to HIPAA.

The biggest transaction of the day reset the value of an email brand. PPC Land reported that Bending Spoons agreed to buy Mailchimp from Intuit for $3.68bn in cash. The Milan-based company, which already owns Vimeo, AOL, Eventbrite and WeTransfer, will pay an enterprise value of $3.68bn, and Intuit will reinvest $368m of the proceeds in new Bending Spoons shares. The price is about 31% of the roughly $12bn Intuit paid in 2021. Bending Spoons describes a playbook of reorganising teams, overhauling technology and pushing monetisation, and says it "has never sold a material business." Mailchimp's domain share fell from 72.68% in January 2022 to 67.54% in May 2024 as Klaviyo climbed, and its current revenue was not disclosed. Closing is expected in early 2027.

Software buyers are getting pickier about growth. PPC Land reported that an ex-Semrush president set a 10% growth floor for martech firms he would buy. Eugene Levin, who led most of Semrush's acquisitions before Adobe's $1.9bn purchase, told the Ahrefs Podcast that he wants companies with $3m to $10m in annual recurring revenue growing at least 10% a year, and will accept breakeven or a 10% margin. He said businesses now trade at two or three times recurring revenue and warned that founder-led firms carry key-person risk: "Smaller companies have much higher dependency on key people, right?" He valued Backlinko's founder-led brand at nothing: "We had to multiply it by zero and that's it."

HubSpot decided how it will charge when AI agents use its software. PPC Land reported that HubSpot won't charge extra when Claude or ChatGPT works its CRM. Everyday use through its connectors and MCP server is included with each seat. "This everyday connector use isn't an extra charge. It comes included with a HubSpot seat," wrote Duncan Lennox. Third-party agents calling existing APIs draw on daily allowances of 250,000 calls for Free and Starter, 650,000 for Professional and 1,000,000 for Enterprise, with capacity packs at $500 a month. Large-scale agent work in a governed environment, still in development, will be billed in credits at $0.010 each. "Every software platform is facing the same decision right now: what to do when AI agents show up at the door," Lennox wrote.

Small advertisers are getting agents of their own. PPC Land reported that InMobi lets seven AI agents run small firms' Google, Meta and ChatGPT ads. InMobi Accelerate plans, builds, launches and measures campaigns across Google Ads, Meta Ads, Microsoft Advertising, TikTok Ads and ChatGPT Ads, and is free to start. "Every plan, creative asset and budget is presented for approval before anything goes live," InMobi says. A commissioned NewtonX survey of 800 US small advertisers and agencies found 93% cannot confidently measure performance across platforms and only 4% can launch a campaign the same day. "AI agents change the economics of expertise," said Rohit Dosi, who runs the product. InMobi did not explain how its single "True ROAS" figure is attributed.

LinkedIn hired a familiar face to sell its ads. Adweek reported that LinkedIn tapped a former Trade Desk executive to lead global ad sales. Anders Mortensen, who left The Trade Desk in June after about seven months as chief revenue officer and joined it from Google, is now vice president of global sales for LinkedIn Ads, reporting to Matthew Derella, senior vice president of LinkedIn Ads and Microsoft Advertising. In his own post he wrote that "AI is changing how people discover brands and make decisions," while "the importance of trust, relationships, and human connection isn't going anywhere."

Google spent the day adjusting the furniture of its results pages. Search Engine Roundtable reported that Google is placing emojis in the AI-generated "What people are saying" box. The emojis come from Google's own AI descriptions rather than the websites it references, and a user named Will spotted the behaviour on Bluesky. Barry Schwartz could replicate it but was cautious about its novelty: "I looked back at my old screenshots of What people are saying and I didn't see emojis in them, but it might not be 100% new."

Two tests touched how Google reinterprets queries and images. Search Engine Roundtable reported that Google is testing a "Show original results" button, which seems to work like the long-standing "Search instead for" link when Google decides a query contains a typo. Khushal Bherwani spotted it; Schwartz could not reproduce it. Search Engine Roundtable also reported that Google Images results now offer a Lens to AI Mode feature, with an icon in the Google app's Images tab that opens an AI Mode chat with the image attached. "It is interesting to see Google keep funneling everything into AI Mode," Schwartz wrote.

Some older tools are disappearing. Search Engine Roundtable reported that Google turned down its Data Feed validation tool, which now returns a 502 error, and replaced the relevant section of its Book actions documentation with a checklist of common errors. "The Data Feed validation tool has been turned down and is no longer available," Google said. Schwartz estimates the tool dated from between 2016 and 2017, when Actions on Google launched.

Publishers who carry Google search ads on their own sites face a single rulebook from January. Search Engine Roundtable reported that Google AdSense is unifying its policies into an AdSense for Search publishers policy, effective January 17, 2027. "AFS ads must only be placed on search results pages," the new text says, and they are barred from pages with no results or placeholder text. Each ad request must come from a user-submitted query, only one request is allowed per user action, ads must appear in one continuous block, and a page may have at most two Google search boxes. AFS slots also cannot be backfilled or alternated with AdSense for Content or Google Ad Manager.

The ads inside AI Mode keep changing shape. PPC News Feed reported that Google is testing a new ad format at the bottom of AI Mode, following an earlier test that placed text-link ads within the content; this version shows more content than previous ones. PPC News Feed also reported that Google is testing blue product names in Shopping ads in AI Mode. The names were previously black, and blue is "typically associated with hyperlinks on Google," which may lift click-through rates. Bing is experimenting too: PPC News Feed reported that Bing is testing a large image ad format on its results page, placed in the centre of the page below Shopping ads, with a prominent "Learn more" button. All three tests were shared by Sachin Patel and reported by Search Engine Watch.

Ranking still decides who gets cited, at least in one category. PPC Land reported that the top pharma search result wins a Google AI Overview citation 69% of the time, in a study by performance.io using Semrush data on about 14,334 US pharma keywords tracked from August 2022 to July 2026. When an AI Overview appeared, the top organic domain was cited 68.8% of the time, and citation rates fell from 69% at position one to 13% at position ten. Pharma brand sites held 9.2% of first-place rankings but only 4.2% of citations, the largest gap of any domain type. "The results are clear: AIOs land ahead of everything else on the SERP 98.63% of the time," the authors wrote, while noting that traffic figures were modelled estimates, not measured clicks.

Being cited, however, is not the same as being recommended. PPC Land reported that Google's AI cited Oasis LMS's own list, then recommended four rivals. A Medium essay by Hordus AI, an AI search services company, drew on Lily Ray's June study of 100 B2B "best" queries, which found that in 224 of 323 citations of a brand's own list, or 69%, the AI Overview did not recommend the brand that wrote it. In the example, an Oasis LMS listicle was cited before Kajabi, Thinkific, LearnWorlds and Teachable were recommended. "The lesson I keep coming back to is that being cited and being recommended are now two different outcomes," the essay's author wrote. PPC Land noted that the essay omitted Ray's September update, which put the figure at 83%.

Two studies questioned how much people shop through chatbots at all. PPC Land reported that only 6.9% of Americans' ChatGPT chats show intent to buy, SparkToro found. Rand Fishkin analysed 118,163 prompts from 12,321 US users of an opt-in panel between January and October. Census-weighted, 4.9% of conversations compared options and 2.1% focused on a specific brand, and Fishkin estimated Google's purchase-related query rate at more than 16 times ChatGPT's. "It's not a search engine. People don't treat it that way," he said. PPC Land flagged inconsistencies between the text and charts. Separately, PPC Land reported that AI chat trails search engines in product research by 17% to 39%, DoubleVerify found: 17% of 22,000 consumers in 21 countries use AI chat to research products, against 39% for search engines and 40% for reviews. Among marketers, 55% rely on platform-native reporting, though DV notes that "a platform's data is the most limited, since it covers only how that platform performed."

The encyclopedia behind many AI answers gained an official badge. PPC Land reported that Wikipedia and Wikidata joined a UN-backed set of six AI building blocks, the DPGs for AI Collection put forward by the Digital Public Goods Alliance and partners including UNICC and ODI. Wikipedia has nearly 260,000 volunteers across more than 300 languages, and SISTRIX has measured it at 12.02% of Google AI Mode citations. "Wikimedia's contribution to responsible AI goes beyond providing freely licensed content and data," the foundation said, though the update said nothing about licensing, API limits or funding.

Microsoft is betting that fewer ads make better ones. PPC Land reported that Microsoft cuts ads per page 35% in its new Discover feed. The feed, on Edge and Windows, shows 35% fewer ads per page than classic MSN, with 35% higher viewability and click-through rates 8% to 12% higher, based on Microsoft's October internal data. The same roundup listed URL inclusions for AI Max final URL expansion, AI content labels for images and video, and an MCP server pilot. Microsoft framed the changes around control and visibility for advertisers using automation. PPC Land noted that the performance figures came only from Microsoft's own data, few included sample sizes, and the 35% viewability gain rests on the same internal measurement.

Google explained how sure advertisers need to be. PPC Land reported that Google says 80% confidence is good enough for directional ad tests, in an Ads Decoded episode on experiments. Al Nevarez, a search experiments specialist, and Sagar Shah, the experiments product lead, recommended starting with templates, running tests for four to six weeks, accepting 80% confidence for directional changes and reserving 95% for major structural ones. "At the end of the day, I guess it's, it basically comes down to going from trust us to prove it," Nevarez said. A budget test runs each arm on half its budget, so a $100 daily budget tested at $150 runs as $50 against $75. Google's own help pages disagree on test length, and advertisers cannot reproduce its calculations.

Google's agents are getting cheaper to run and easier to set loose. PPC Land reported that Google shrinks idle tools in Gemini agents to about 26 tokens each, through Tool Retrieval, a preview in the Gemini API that keeps most tool definitions out of each prompt until needed. The design closely matches approaches from Anthropic and OpenAI, down to a shared defer_loading flag. "Sending every full parameter schema on every request adds up fast," Google wrote, though loaded schemas keep incurring charges and Google published no savings figures. PPC Land also reported that Gemini can now operate Mac apps in a background window, from $4.99. Computer use in the Gemini app clicks, types and fills forms across desktop software and websites for US adults on AI Plus, Pro or Ultra plans, while the user keeps the main screen. Google has not said how the agent identifies itself to websites, which matters for site owners reading their traffic.

Google's top AI plan now removes more viewers from YouTube's ad audience. PPC Land reported that Google's $99.99 AI plan now spares up to five more people YouTube ads, after the YouTube benefit in Google AI Ultra was upgraded from Premium Individual to Premium Family. One subscriber can extend ad-free YouTube and YouTube Music to five other household members, so each Ultra subscription can remove up to six accounts from the ad-supported audience rather than one. The standalone Family plan costs $26.99 a month in the US. Alphabet reported more than 150 million YouTube Music and Premium subscribers in October, but has not disclosed Ultra numbers.

The plumbing of programmatic advertising is about to show more pipes. PPC Land reported that ad buyers face longer supply chains under IAB Tech Lab's schain 1.1. The updated SupplyChain object now lists companies that take custody of a bid request even if they never handle payment. "Supply Chain 1.1 is now live and discloses any entity that has custody of the bid request," said Hillary Slattery of IAB Tech Lab. Buyers who count hops for supply path optimisation should expect longer chains, and validation rules for the new nodes will not be finished until early 2027. A HUMAN Security diagnostic found only 42% of schain-carrying requests passed full validation.

The way television is measured is shifting as fast as the way it is watched. PPC Land reported that cable dropped to 31.7% of US TV ad time, the lowest in Comscore's series. In Comscore's September Score Report, broadcast rose to 45.5% of in-home ad exposure time, cable fell 2.8 points to 31.7%, and streaming reached a series high of 22.8%. Disney ABC moved from sixth to first among owners at 10.0%, and Hulu passed Tubi among streaming services. The report "measures advertising exposure, not overall content consumption," Comscore cautioned, a different lens from Nielsen's viewing figures.

Radio is changing its stopwatch. PPC Land reported that one minute will be enough for Nielsen to credit a radio listener. From the April 2027 survey, Nielsen's Portable People Meter qualifier falls from three minutes to one per quarter-hour, its second cut in under two years, and Nielsen expects about 20% more measurable ad impressions. "Adopting a 1-minute qualifier strengthens data for everyone," said Rich Tunkel, managing director of Nielsen Audio. PPC Land calculated that a 20% impression gain at flat cost would cut CPMs by about 16.7%, and warned that part of any rise next spring will reflect methodology rather than more listening.

Broadcasters are selling outcomes as well as audiences. PPC Land reported that Sky Media shifts addressable TV ads to the homes that respond mid-campaign with Outcomes Accelerator, unveiled at its 2027 Showcase in London. Plans draw on a databank of 2,400 addressable campaigns from more than 500 advertisers, and household data then moves delivery towards responsive homes. Sky also signed Platform Media, 1071 Media and Goalhanger, the publisher behind The Rest Is Football. "Audiences don't think in platforms," said Pippa Scaife, Sky Media's director of digital advertising. Pricing and beta results were not disclosed.

Live sport remains television's safest sale. Adweek reported that Disney Advertising hopes to give brands multiple layups this college basketball season, with more than 6,000 regular-season games across ESPN, ESPN+, the ACC Network and SEC Network, and exclusive coverage of the Players Era Tournament for the first time. More than half of last year's 200 advertisers are back and Disney added more than 20 new ones. ESPN had its most-watched men's regular season in 11 years, with viewership up 25%. "College sports fans choose their team once and stay for life, which makes them really rare for audiences and brands," said Jacqueline Dobies, vice president of revenue and yield management, who said combined revenue is pacing double digits ahead.

Car makers want streaming television to prove it sells cars. PPC Land reported that only 18% of auto advertisers say CTV reports show cars sold, Jamloop found. In a survey of 120 automotive advertisers, 73% use their own sales data or registration records to target streaming ads, 63% consider vehicle sales a key success measure and 77% plan to spend more on connected TV. PPC Land noted that the survey's methodology was undisclosed and that Jamloop sells sales-based measurement. Google offered its own proof point: PPC Land reported that Google says DV360 vertical video cut Ford's cost per unique user 19%, with 26% more unique reach, in its monthly Google Marketing Platform "Drop," which also added Google audiences on Spotify in the US and India and Loblaw Advance to its Commerce Media Suite. No baseline, budget or method was given for the Ford figures.

Nike wants more people to count as athletes, and more creators to speak for it. Digiday reported inside Nike's plan to turn creators into brand builders. At its November 17 investor day, chief executive Eliott Hill set out a strategy called Full Stride Ahead and broadened the brand's definition of an athlete: "When we say athlete, we mean athlete in the broadest sense possible." Brand president Amy Montagne said marketing spend will shift towards grassroots efforts and local creators, reaching "the right people, in the right places and at the right moments," while big campaigns continue. The Studio Fleece launch used more than 100 athletes, entertainers, creators and stylists, the World Cup campaign drew 5.7 billion content views, and Nike targets about $5bn of extra revenue by fiscal 2031. Creator pay and ownership of their work were not on the agenda.

Publishers want to keep the creators they make famous. Digiday reported that Mail Metro Media's next creator play is representing them. The Daily Mail's ad sales arm is building an in-house talent agency, aiming to be in market by the end of 2026, after creator deals grew from about GBP5,000 each to seven figures. "The huge risk is that we make these people super famous and then they go and get signed by a different agent," said Hannah Blake, managing director of creator and new media. The unit draws 5 billion monthly video views across 10 brands, its creators are salaried, and the company owns the intellectual property they develop.

Not every creator-led campaign is welcome. PPC Land reported that Ultra faces TINA.org complaints over a 32m-view "Zyn and Adderall" ad. Truth in Advertising asked the FTC, the FDA, New York's attorney general and New York City's consumer department to examine Ultra, which sells nicotine-free focus pouches. It alleges the company promotes them as an ADHD treatment and Adderall substitute without approval or substantiation, and that ads and gaming creators reach minors. A co-founder had described the product on TikTok as being as if "Zyn and Adderall had a baby." "Ultra doesn't bury its Adderall marketing comparison. It headlines it," TINA.org wrote. These are allegations, and no investigation has been opened.

Generative AI is creating new disputes over likeness. PPC Land reported that a model sued RomperJack after his 2021 photos became AI-generated Instagram ads. Jeffrey Stanfield, a Los Angeles model and actor, alleges that after the clothing brand changed hands in 2025, the new owner used generative AI to create ad images and a video of him from a shoot for which he was paid in clothing. The complaint pleads false endorsement under the Lanham Act and California publicity claims. "Defendants could have requested a written release from Mr. Stanfield before using his identity. They did not," it says. These are allegations, and the company removed the content after a demand letter.

AI is also moving deeper into regulated health. Adweek reported that ChatGPT is going from healthcare advice to a prescriptions platform. Photon, a digital prescription network, launched a plugin on November 16 that lets US clinicians using ChatGPT for Clinicians or ChatGPT for Healthcare write, check and send prescriptions inside the chat, after verifying each one. "The goal is to take administrative work off the clinician's plate so they can focus on care," said Otto Sipe, Photon's chief executive. Patients then get a link to compare pharmacies. OpenAI is allowing more healthcare advertising and says it does not use health data for targeted ads.

Apple handed app developers a privacy switch. PPC Land reported that Apple lets iOS 27 apps tell websites not to sell or share user data. A new WebKit API lets apps built on WKWebView or SwiftUI's WebPage send the Global Privacy Control signal, which California treats as a legal opt-out. It is off by default, and each app must add its own setting; once enabled, the signal reaches subframes and subresources, so third-party ad tags receive it. John Wilander of WebKit documented the change on November 18, and PPC Land linked it to recent enforcement, including Hertz's $1.55m fine in California. In a separate change, PPC Land reported that Apple's Safari preview stops losing analytics beacons when pages close. Safari Technology Preview 257 fixed beacons sent during pagehide, the moment analytics and ad scripts often send final session data, among 201 changes.

The same signal sits at the centre of a first-of-its-kind settlement. PPC Land reported that Polaris will pay $150,000 in Minnesota's first data privacy law case. The powersports maker's website allegedly refused opt-outs when consumers did not answer a verification email and ignored Global Privacy Control signals on pages already open. California's regulator is collecting a separate $910,986 fine under a parallel order, and another $150,000 is stayed. Polaris must audit its trackers quarterly for three years, and it denies the allegations. "Once sold, that data can be sold again, and again," the attorney general's office said.

States are also tightening the contracts behind data sharing. AdExchanger reported why companies should not give privacy regulators an excuse to come knocking, from an IAB event on state privacy laws. Delaware's HB 380, effective January 1, 2027, requires companies to verify, at least through questionnaires and document reviews, that a partner can meet its privacy obligations before sharing personal data. John Eakins, Delaware's deputy attorney general, said ad tech's scale is no excuse and each transfer needs its own contract, "because each hop is a transaction involving personal data." Michael Hahn of the IAB warned that custom questionnaires from every company in a programmatic chain would create paperwork without improving safety. Eakins called it a pet peeve when privacy policies omit Delaware from their list of states.

Spain's regulator issued two warnings for marketers. PPC Land reported that Spain's AEPD says marketing chiefs cannot double as data protection officers. A 59-page guide treats the head of marketing as, as a rule, incompatible with the role, because that person shapes the purposes of processing and would supervise their own decisions. It also warns that "a bonus or variable remuneration linked to financial results or business profit could also affect their independence." PPC Land also reported on Barca's EUR500,000 fine, in which Spain says a risk report is not a DPIA. The AEPD's new legal criterion, drawn from its fine against FC Barcelona over a biometric membership census of about 143,000 members, holds that a risk analysis cannot automatically substitute for a data protection impact assessment. "Risk analyses are not a mere document or a mere formality," the AEPD said.

Courts in two countries ruled against secrecy and against Google. PPC Land reported that Google lost its bid to overturn Colombia's under-18 data consent orders. A Bogota administrative tribunal upheld three orders from the SIC, Colombia's regulator, holding that cookies and identifiers on Colombian devices count as local collection even though Google has no Colombian office, and requiring proof of parental authorisation for every user under 18. The court found Family Link leaves out teenagers aged 13 to 17. In London, PPC Land reported that the Home Office lost its bid to hide that it served Apple a secret notice. The Investigatory Powers Tribunal found officials had already confirmed the technical capability notice to newspapers, observing that "anyone with even a passing interest in this topic already knows." Most of Apple's challenge can now be argued in open court.

Election infrastructure faced intruders rather than floods. PPC Land reported that voting sites faced 180 times more hack attempts than DDoS attacks, Cloudflare found. Across more than 1,400 election-related sites in the midterm cycle, daily exploit attempts rose from 200,000 in January to 2 million in October, and Cloudflare mitigated 392 million such attacks in the year before the vote. "Cloudflare did not record a single significant distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack" on state and local election sites on Election Day, when their traffic peaked at about 602 million requests. The post did not say whether any intrusion succeeded.

Child safety became a commercial issue for two platforms. Digiday reported that advertisers suspended TikTok activity in response to a Spanish CSAM investigation. After the fact-checker Maldita.es found abusive videos, or promoted sites selling such material, near ads from 21 brands, Santander paused its campaigns, the energy company Moeve reportedly followed, and Spain's public prosecution office opened an investigation. "Until we know what's happening, it's better to pause," said Laura Camazon of Mediaplus Equmedia, whose three affected clients will likely stay off until 2027. "We condemn child sexual abuse and exploitation," a TikTok spokesperson said, adding that a task force is handling the reports.

In Washington, PPC Land reported that Roblox's 14,000-word terms bind children to arbitration, a Senate panel heard. Witnesses targeted a binding, confidential arbitration clause the company is using to move child exploitation lawsuits out of public court. "I never expected to appear before this body to describe the use of forced arbitration against nine-year-olds," said Myriam Gilles, a Northwestern law professor. Reports of child exploitation reached 65,381 in 2025, up from 675 in 2019. Roblox did not testify and called the claims misleading.

Meta is testing a messaging app with stricter defaults for strangers. PPC Land reported that Instagram is testing Direct, a chat app that needs no Instagram account, in Turkiye and Thailand. People without an Instagram account can be messaged only by their contacts, the minimum age is 13, and teens keep Teen Account protections. Instagram tried a Direct app once before, testing it from December 2017 and pulling it in May 2019. The announcement said nothing about encryption, advertising or business messaging.

Australia set the terms for wagering ads online. PPC Land reported that Australia bans wagering ads for logged-out users from January 1, 2027. Platforms escape the ban only through a "triple lock": reasonable steps to keep out restricted users, a registered logged-in account, and an account-based opt-out. Restricted users include anyone under 18, anyone unverified, anyone logged out and anyone who opted out, so an anonymous adult counts too. "There is no one-size-fits-all approach for what constitutes taking reasonable steps," the regulator said. The same market is worrying about who learns the trade. PPC Land reported that eight of 12 search recruiters surveyed by IAB Australia expect fewer junior roles, with 92% reporting more demand for AI skills. "We can automate the task, but we can't automate the learning," the paper said.

Bot management is the set of tools and policies a site uses to decide, request by request, what each automated visitor may do. Imperva's Bad Bot Report put automated traffic at more than 53% of all web traffic in 2025, and Cloudflare began blocking AI crawlers by default for new customers on July 1, 2025.

Referrer policy is the browser rule that sets how much of a page's address is shared when the browser requests another resource. Chrome 85 adopted strict-origin-when-cross-origin as its default in August 2020, and on May 23, 2025 Google called the referrer stripping on AI Mode links a bug.

Server logs record every request a web server receives, including bots that never run analytics tags. Microsoft Clarity launched a Bot Activity dashboard built on server-side log collection on January 21, 2026.

Referral exclusion tells an analytics tool to ignore referring domains such as payment processors, so an ad click is not overwritten when a shopper returns from a payment page. GA4 launched on October 14, 2020 with referral handling rebuilt at the data stream level.

Core update is a broad change Google makes several times a year to the systems that rank search results. Google released the November 2026 core update on November 10, 2026, with a rollout of up to two weeks.
